0.note: The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

1.note: David is using the term **day** to refer to a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when you experience trouble] or [in time of trouble]

David is using the term **name** to represent the person and character of God himself, including his attributes and covenant faithfulness to deliver his people when they call on him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the God of Jacob]

David is speaking of Yahweh protecting his anointed king as if Yahweh would **set** him up on a **high** place where his enemies could not reach and harm him. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may … keep you safe] or [may … keep you from being harmed by your enemies]

2.note: David assumes that readers will know that **help** means military assistance or deliverance from enemies. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [May he help you prevail against your adversaries with aid]

David assumes that readers will know that **the sanctuary** refers to the temple in Jerusalem, the place where God’s presence dwells. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [May he send you help from his sanctuary, the Temple]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [May he send you help from the sanctuary, yes, may he support you from Zion]

3.note: David assumes that readers will know that when God remembers someone’s offerings, he acts favorably toward that person based on those offerings. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [May he take notice of all of your offerings and act accordingly]

David is using **regard as fat** as a common expression of his culture to mean “accept” or “be pleased with.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly as in the UST.

4.note: Here the **heart** represents where a person’s desires exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what you desire] or [the desires of your heart]

David assumes that readers will understand that **your heart** refers to the king’s desires or wishes. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [according to your heart’s desire]

5.note: In this context, the forms of the two verbs the ULT translates as **We will shout for joy** and **we will set up our banners** could indicate: (1) a resolution of the will and therefore be translated as in the ULT, or (2) a request. Alternate translation: [May we shout for joy … may we set up our banners]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **joy** and **salvation**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [When you save us, then we will joyfully shout]

Here David is using the term **name** to represent who God is or to refer to his reputation. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and for the glory of our God]

A **banner** is a flag made from a large piece of cloth that is attached to a long pole. People, groups, and kings had their own unique banners by which they identified themselves. If your readers would not be familiar with this type of flag, you could use the name of something similar in your area, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [we will set up our flags]

Raising banners was a symbolic action by which armies showed victory. In this context it was done in order to give God the glory for helping the soldiers of the Israelite army defeat their enemies. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and in the name of our God we will raise our banners to celebrate the victory Yahweh has given us]

6.note: You may be used to indicating when David is referring to himself in the third person by saying something such as “me, his anointed.” However, we recommend that you not do that in this instance, since the term **anointed** here refers to others besides David.

David assumes that readers will know that **his anointed** refers to the king of Israel, whom God had chosen and set apart by anointing with oil. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [his anointed king]

The expression **his anointed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [the one whom he had anointed]

Here, **right hand** represents the power of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with mighty deeds by his great power to save]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with mighty deeds of his saving right hand]

7.note: David is using **These in chariots and these in horses** as a common expression of his culture to mean “Some trust in chariots and some in horses” or “Some trust in chariots and others in horses.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Some in chariots and some in horses] or [Some trust in chariots and others trust in horses]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [These trust in chariots and these trust in horses]

David assumes that readers will know that chariots and horses were military equipment that symbolized military power and strength. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [These trust in their military chariots and these in their war horses]

David uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between those who trust in military power and those who trust in Yahweh. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [however, we] or [in contrast, we]

David assumes that readers will know that remembering the name of Yahweh means trusting in him and calling on him for help. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [will keep in mind] or [will be confident in]

David is using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is and his character which includes being very powerful. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh our God] or [Yahweh our powerful God]

8.note: The pronoun **They** refers to those who trust in chariots and horses (mentioned in the previous verse), while the pronoun **we** refers to David and those who trust in Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Those who trust in those things … but we who trust in Yahweh]

David assumes that readers will know that **bow down and fall** refers to being defeated in battle. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [They collapse and fall in battle]
Here, **fall** represents dying in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and fall dead]

9.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, please save]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, save the king] or [Yahweh, save us, your people]
The word the ULT translates as **the king** could belong: (1) with the second line, as in the ULT, or (2) with the first line. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, save the king! May he answer us]
David is using the term **day** to refer to a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [at the time] or [when]
